prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength lattice to systematic uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B061 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and after the full exchange my reasons are sharper than in round 1. The criterion I would make explicit, since the chair's summary asks for one, is this: the committee should first ask whether the claimed achievement is complete, independently confirmed and capable of being cited as one thing, and only then weigh how new the regime is. On that test B061 is the strongest. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts for a large neutral-atom ensemble, and Ye's group brought strontium lattice clocks to 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and into the many-body regime. Lindroth, who can judge the polarisability and blackbody-shift physics directly, confirms that these steps are sound physics and not only engineering. Several independent laboratories reproduce the performance and cross-institute comparisons test it. The consequences are already measured: millimetre-scale redshift tests, constraints on varying constants and the basis for the redefinition of the second. On the overlap question the chair asks, I read the 2005 prize as honouring the comb and precision laser spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize as honouring control and measurement of individual quantum systems including ion clocks. Neither citation covers the magic-wavelength optical lattice or the ensemble clock, so a citation worded on the neutral-atom optical lattice clock and silent on ion-clock priority does not repeat either prize. I do not claim this settles the disagreement with the B013 camp; it is a different judgement about what the prize should weigh, and I state it as mine.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged in kind but I now weigh it a little more heavily. B061 is a precision-measurement advance, and a reasonable member can hold that a new regime of nature, which is what B013 is, should outrank a new level of accuracy in a field the prize has honoured in 2005 and 2012. Attribution is clean at two names only because the three-person limit and the citation wording exclude Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and Olsson's question whether the 10^-18 milestones belong to Ye alone or to a wider group is not fully answered by saying that Ye drove the programme; I cannot show from my own knowledge that no one else's contribution was decisive. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the payoff is still prospective. If the committee adopts novelty of regime as its first criterion, B013 is the better prize and I would not resist that on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Moved from B008 to B013 and argues that the three credited names map onto the decisive prediction and the decisive experimental programme, while conceding that the pairing mechanism is contested and that B061 is the more finished alternative.
responses.response: I agree with your own last sentence, and it is close to my whole case: if the committee judges moire physics too young or the credit too contested, B061 is the more finished choice. On Bistritzer I accept your argument that dropping him severs the 2011 prediction, which means that my earlier willingness to entertain a two-name MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero version was too easy; if B013 is chosen, the three-name set is the version I could defend. Where we still differ is on what the prize should weight first. You weigh the opening of a new regime; I weigh completeness and confirmation of the claim. I do not think either is wrong, but I would ask you whether the unsettled pairing mechanism would worry you more if the citation mentioned superconductivity at all, because that wording choice decides how much of the maturity risk the prize takes on.

responses.point: Asks that the omission of Cao, Dean and the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists be stated openly if B013 is chosen, and describes the prediction-then-observation structure as the strongest discovery case on the shortlist.
responses.response: I agree that a prediction followed by an experimental discovery is the best form a discovery can take, and I concede that B013 has this structure more clearly than B061, where the concept and the demonstration were closer together in time and were developed in parallel by several groups. I also agree that the omissions should be stated openly, and I would apply the same standard to B061, where Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the national-laboratory groups are likewise outside the pair. Where I part from you is on readiness. You list the correlated and superconducting states as still moving; I take that as a reason to prefer a result whose central claim does not depend on how those states are eventually explained. For B013 I would then still want the citation to rest on flat bands and the existence of correlated states, not on a mechanism.

responses.point: Places B013 first as a discovery nature delivered, notes that Cao and Fatemi are outside the three names, and asks whether the unsettled pairing mechanism is a maturity concern or only follow-on physics.
responses.response: On your direct question I now lean to the second reading: the existence of the flat-band platform and the correlated insulators does not depend on the pairing mechanism, so for B013 the mechanism is mostly a citation-wording matter and I withdraw part of my round-1 maturity worry. The credit problem is the larger obstacle for me, because Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 experiments and Fatemi are outside the list, and a three-person limit cannot repair that. You also asked in your round-1 file how much weight a few years of moire proliferation should carry against decades of confirmation; I would give it substantial weight, but I do not treat age as disqualifying, and for me it is not the deciding factor. The deciding factor is that the B061 claim is complete and its attribution is shorter to defend.

responses.point: Rests the B061 case on atomic-structure physics she can judge directly, and says that if the committee wants a prize that opens a new field of physics rather than a new level of measurement, B013 is the stronger candidate on that criterion.
responses.response: Your atomic-structure argument remains the one I find most persuasive, since it is an expert check on exactly the part I cannot verify myself as an astroparticle experimentalist. I also think your last sentence in the case against is the honest statement of the committee's real disagreement. The chair's summary asks for an explicit criterion; I propose confirmation and completeness first, novelty of regime second, and I accept that this ordering is a judgement and not a finding. On credit I take your point that PTB, SYRTE and others contributed. I would draw the citation around the lattice clock concept and its demonstrated 10^-18 performance and not around who first reached each milestone, so that the citation does not adjudicate a priority dispute that the committee cannot settle.

responses.point: Supports B061 as the convergent choice, discloses a research stay in the Hall laboratory and training under Svanberg, and notes that the redefinition of the second has not happened yet and that waiting until next year is possible.
responses.response: I have noted your disclosure for the record, and I agree it is a lineage and not a collaboration with Katori or Ye. I would add that Lindroth and Olsson reach the same ranking without that lineage, so the case does not rest on your vote. On timing, I do not think the pending redefinition argues for waiting: the prize recognises the demonstrated performance and the invention, and the redefinition is a consequence that metrology bodies decide on their own schedule, which the committee should not make a precondition. I would ask you the converse: if the committee judges that the redefinition should come first, does your case for B061 weaken, or does it stay the same because the experimental record is already complete?

responses.point: Prefers B034 for conceptual originality and the cleanest credit, concedes that B013 and B061 have broader support, and asks what would make a citation narrow enough to avoid the 2012 experimental record.
responses.response: I accept that Cirac and Zoller have the cleanest two-name credit on the list, and I would not dispute their influence. My difficulty is the one the chair's summary records: the 2012 prize and the 2022 prize recognised much of the experimental ground the proposals opened, and a citation narrow enough to avoid them risks describing only a subset of what the theory contributed. You said what would persuade you to move; in return, I would be persuaded to rank B034 higher by a citation you could draft in one sentence that names a single achievement and does not mention ions, cold atoms and simulation together. I could not write one, which is why I keep it behind B061 and B013.

responses.point: Moved to B061 and asks whether the 10^-18 milestones belong to Ye alone or to a wider group, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or others have claims that make two names unfair.
responses.response: I cannot answer that fully, and I would rather say so than assert it. My view is that Katori has the conceptual claim through the magic-wavelength lattice and that Ye's group has the decisive demonstration of 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and many-body clock operation, but the comparisons across NIST, PTB and SYRTE show that the performance is a field result and not Ye's alone. That is a real weakness for a two-name prize, and it is the main reason I list my own reservation first. If the committee thinks it fatal, the right response is B013, not a third name added to B061. You also asked in round 1 about the credit rule for B009; I have not changed my view that B009 is harder on attribution than B061 and I do not press it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that confirmation and completeness should rank ahead of novelty of regime; I hold this ordering as a judgement and I expect reasonable colleagues to reverse it.

Whether the neutral-atom optical lattice clock is read as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, and whether a narrow citation can avoid any claim on ion-clock priority.

Whether two names fairly capture the lattice-clock record given the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups; I rely on recollection of the history and not on verified sources.

Whether B013 is better credited with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, or whether Cao and Fatemi should enter; I cannot resolve this and I would not vote against B013 on credit alone if my colleagues find a principled rule.
B009 remains in my alternatives out of field familiarity; I have moved it down on attribution and source-identification grounds and I defer to colleagues on its weight.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my documented record for B061 or B013: my collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) do not include the lattice-clock, moire or IceCube communities, and I have no recorded tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. B009 lies in my own field of astroparticle physics, so I list it only as an alternative and I would recuse myself from deciding it. I support Kroll's disclosure of his Hall-laboratory lineage being kept in the record and I note that it does not change my reading. As chair I record that I have tried to weigh B061 and B013 on a stated criterion and not on the support counts.
